name: Madagascar
card_headline: Madagascar's military-led government plans a referendum in mid-2027 and a presidential vote by year end, but its national consultation is late and power cuts continue
card_summary: Colonel Michael Randrianirina has led Madagascar since 17 October 2025, after soldiers joined Gen Z protests over power and water cuts and President Andry Rajoelina fled. [1] The timetable has a constitutional referendum between May and July 2027 and a presidential election before year end. [2] The African Union suspended Madagascar; SADC did not, but in June it called for the release of political prisoners. [3][4] The IPC projects 3.72 million people in acute food insecurity by February 2027. [5]
card_local: L'Express and Newsmada report that the national consultation is behind schedule, that the High Constitutional Court backs a referendum before the presidential vote, and that SADC elders liked the preparations. Midi Madagasikara reports power cuts a year on. [2][6][7]
card_international: AFP reports that Gen Z activists say the new government uses the old tactics, and Reuters and AFP reported the March dismissal of the cabinet and the naming of a new prime minister. [1][8][9]
card_scholar: ISS calls the takeover a 'coupvolution' and warns that juntas elsewhere usually miss their deadlines, and Amnesty reports a return of authoritarian practices. [10][11]
context_md: Gen Z protests began on 25 September 2025 over water and power cuts and spread to complaints about corruption and poverty. [12][3] The UN human rights office counted at least 22 deaths in the first days, and blamed security forces for some of them. [13] Colonel Michael Randrianirina's CAPSAT unit joined the protesters, Rajoelina left the country and was impeached by lawmakers, and the African Union suspended Madagascar. [3] Randrianirina was sworn in on 17 October 2025 and promised elections within two years. [1] He rejects the word coup and says the Constitutional Court transferred power to him. [9] SADC did not suspend Madagascar, which ISS calls a gamble. [10] About 80 percent of Malagasy live on less than $2.15 a day, according to World Bank data cited by AFP. [12]

sections.title: The calendar now runs referendum first, presidential vote second, and the consultation is already late
sections.body_md:
Colonel Michael Randrianirina commanded the CAPSAT army unit before his soldiers joined the Gen Z protests and Andry Rajoelina fled. He was sworn in as head of state on 17 October 2025. [1][3] He rejects the coup label and says the Constitutional Court transferred power to him. [9] L'Express reports the current timetable as a constitutional referendum between May and July 2027, two presidential rounds before the end of 2027, and a new president in early 2028. [2] Voters would be summoned 90 days before the referendum. [14]

The High Constitutional Court said in an opinion of 4 November that the referendum should come first, and that any draft constitution needs three-quarters of the National Assembly before it goes to voters. [2][14] At the opening of a preparatory dialogue at Ivato, Randrianirina said elections will be held in 2027 and that 95 percent of proposals from earlier consultations favour a referendum. The 95 percent figure is his own. Asked whether he will run, he said his mission is to guide the Refondation and the electoral process. [15] AFP notes that he and the former president Marc Ravalomanana are expected to run. [12] In October he told UN Radio he believes the calendar can be kept, and that the voter list should be revised by April 2027 if all goes well. [16]

The weak point is the national consultation led by the FFKM, the council of Christian churches. On 8 November in Antsirabe the colonel called it slightly late. L'Express reports that the FFKM plans to publish its resolutions only after May 2027, which is close to the opening of the referendum window. [2][14] The state has set aside 32 billion ariary for it. [6] Cabinet turnover has been abrupt: Randrianirina dismissed the prime minister and every minister on 9 March without explanation, and on 15 March named Mamitiana Rajaonarison, who had led the financial intelligence unit SAMIFIN since 2021. [8][9]

lenses.local: L'Express and Newsmada carry the timetable, the court opinion and the consultation delay; L'Express attributes the 1 November statement that the referendum comes first to a minister speaking on the state broadcaster TVM, which RSF describes as controlled by government directives. [2][15][17]
lenses.international: AFP reports that drafting of the constitution is stalled and that elections are now pledged for late 2027. [12]
lenses.scholar: ISS says juntas elsewhere have usually missed promised deadlines and that the March dismissal raises doubts about Randrianirina's commitment, while Georgetown's student review argues he may extend military rule if the timetable gives him no advantage. [10][18]

sections.title: The AU suspended Madagascar and SADC did not, and both now press on prisoners and the calendar
sections.body_md:
The African Union suspended Madagascar in October 2025, and the UN said it was deeply concerned by an unconstitutional change of power. [3] The AU Peace and Security Council met on 10 March 2026, welcomed the Refondation programme presented on 28 February, and urged scrupulous respect for the 24-month calendar. It also voiced concern over the dismissal of the prime minister, called for the unconditional release of political detainees, and announced a field mission. An AU envoy said in February that sanctions would be lifted only after the presidential election. [19] This draft did not find the outcome of the field mission.

SADC took a softer line. ISS describes the decision not to suspend as a gamble and says the bloc should be ready to suspend if the roadmap is not followed. Its December 2025 summit required a report and draft roadmap by 28 February, which Randrianirina submitted. [10] SADC's executive secretary, Elias Magosi, visited on 20 January. [20] On 29 June an extraordinary summit chaired by Cyril Ramaphosa, with Randrianirina attending, called for the release of political prisoners, an end to arbitrary arrests of opposition leaders and Gen Z members, and the return of exiles. It drew on three assessment missions between October 2025 and May 2026. [4]

In August Randrianirina told Ramaphosa in Durban that the first electoral deadline is July 2027. [21] In November a SADC delegation led by the former Malawian president Joyce Banda told Newsmada it was encouraged by preparations, and Randrianirina received it at Iavoloha on 9 November. [6] L'Express says UN, AU and SADC envoys reportedly voiced concern about the delay. [14] AFP reports that Madagascar keeps its ties with France while building a military partnership with Russia, including training by Africa Corps. [12]

lenses.local: Midi Madagasikara reported SADC's January visit and L'Express reported the AU's March communiqué. [20][19]
lenses.international: RFI reports that the June SADC communiqué was sharper than earlier statements, since SADC had not suspended Madagascar. [4]
lenses.scholar: ISS argues that having declined to suspend, SADC carries a special duty to monitor the roadmap. [10]

sections.title: Gen Z leaders face state-security charges, and rights groups report about twenty political detainees
sections.body_md:
The protesters who forced out Rajoelina now complain of the same tools. AFP reports that after a march in April several activists were arrested under a charge of endangering state security, which allows 15 days of detention, and that Herizo Andriamanantena, 30, spent 13 days in police custody and lost his job. [1] L'Express describes a demonstration of about 100 people at Place du 13 Mai on 11 April and four young people held at the criminal brigade. It relays a TV5 Monde report that some detainees were questioned at gunpoint. The police director general said one woman was not subjected to violence. [22]

Amnesty's November assessment counts at least 20 people arbitrarily detained for political reasons, including the former presidential candidates Sylvain Rabetsaroana and Paul Rabary Andrianirina. It says at least nine Gen Z leaders were arrested in April and three remain in provisional detention. It adds that no serious investigation has followed the shootings of protesters in 2025, and that a cybercrime bill proposed in August would widen state access to online data. [11] RFI reports that about twenty people linked to the former regime are being prosecuted, and an Amnesty opinion piece from March says affiliates of the former regime have faced arrests under a broad national-security charge. [4][23] On the accountability side, AFP reports that a court sentenced the former security official Richard Ravalomanana to 10 years of hard labour on 1 September, and that a trial has started for Rajoelina's ally Mamy Ravatomanga over a Boeing transfer to Iran. [12]

RSF ranks Madagascar 103rd of 180 in 2026, up from 113th. It says the state broadcasters RNM and TVM are largely controlled by government directives, that the regulator ANRCM is not yet operational, and that an access-to-information law has been pending for 16 years. [17] This draft read no reply from the government to Amnesty's findings.

lenses.local: L'Express reported the April arrests and Amnesty's reaction within days. [22]
lenses.international: AFP interviewed detained activists and lawyers a year after the takeover. [1]
lenses.scholar: Amnesty warns that without regional and international pressure Madagascar risks a familiar cycle of authoritarian practice, and IDOS says youth protests can topple a regime without guaranteeing democratic reform. [11][24]

sections.title: Jirama still cuts power and water, and the IMF has released money while inflation climbs
sections.body_md:
Load-shedding sparked the uprising and has not ended. Midi Madagasikara reported that a power cut hit a Gen Z photo exhibition in early October while the president was speaking, and that residents sometimes face cuts of up to four hours a day. [7] Energy Minister Radonirina Rabearimanga blamed the 2026 drought for a water shortage at the Andekaleka hydro plant, and Jirama ran a three-day cloud-seeding operation. Jirama's director general Hajatiana Rasolomanana said the outages affect Antananarivo, Diego and Toamasina, and Jirama has an offer of 207 MW of solar power below 8.5 US cents. [25] In August he said contracts no longer suited to current conditions will be reviewed and that load-shedding will not fully disappear this year. [26] Residents reported in May that a jerrican of water cost 3,000 ariary, up from 500. [27]

An L'Express commentary argues the problem is financial, not technical: Jirama pays for declared capacity that it says is often at least double what private suppliers deliver. It says Antsiranana needs 11 MW and receives 3 MW, and that the president gave one supplier a week to fix supply. [28] That account rests on one article.

On 30 September the IMF Board completed the third and fourth reviews of the ECF and RSF arrangements and released about $155 million. It put growth at 3.1 percent in 2025 and 3.8 percent in 2026, inflation at 9.3 percent at end 2026, the 2026 current account deficit at 8.3 percent of GDP and public debt at 49.3 percent of GDP. It says tax collection fell well short and asks for full fuel price adjustment by January 2027. [29] In September AFP reported that about $180 million in IMF-related funds had been frozen over fuel subsidies; this draft did not establish whether that is the same money. [12] A Gen Z spokesperson says 36 percent of Malagasy have electricity, and IDOS cites World Bank data of 39 percent. [30][24]

lenses.local: Midi Madagasikara and L'Express cover the outages, the drought explanation and the contract review. [7][25][26]
lenses.international: AFP reports that the government used fuel subsidies to hold down prices and that activists say water and power demands are unmet. [12]
lenses.scholar: The IMF is the main source on growth, inflation and debt, and asks for a Jirama recovery plan that limits calls on the budget. [29]

sections.title: El Nino threatens a southern hunger crisis that the IPC puts at 3.7 million people by February
sections.body_md:
The IPC snapshot published on 15 July 2026 counts about 2.57 million people in Phase 3 or worse in March to May 2026. It projects 3.72 million for October 2026 to February 2027, including about 426,000 in Phase 4. All Phase 4 pockets are in the Grand South, and Androy has about 589,000 people in Phase 3 or worse, nearly 48 percent of its analysed population. About 502,000 children aged 6 to 59 months face acute malnutrition between May 2026 and April 2027, 78,000 of them severe. [5]

FEWS NET expects an early lean season in the Grand South, with El Nino likely to delay the October rains and farm labour income 20 to 40 percent below average. It adds that higher fuel, freight and import costs will push food prices up. [31] L'Express reports that the World Food Programme has begun anticipatory action in Bekily, Ambovombe, Beloha, Tsihombe and Antanimora Sud, and quotes the economist Eddy Rinah Ramananandro of CREM warning of effects on rice, cassava and maize. It gives no funding figures. [32] Midi Madagasikara warns of a possible extreme El Nino comparable to 1982 and of internal displacement. [33]

Earlier figures were lower. In January Midi Madagasikara reported that nearly 1.64 million people could be affected by April 2026, using an IPC document published in September 2025. [34] The two analyses cover different periods and this draft did not reconcile them.

lenses.local: L'Express and Midi Madagasikara carry the IPC numbers, the WFP action and the El Nino warning. [32][33]
lenses.scholar: The IPC and FEWS NET are the technical sources, and both describe drought, high prices and poor harvests as the drivers. [5][31]

timeline.text: Gen Z protests begin over water and power cuts.
The UN human rights office reports at least 22 dead and more than 100 injured and blames security forces for some deaths.
The African Union suspends Madagascar after the CAPSAT unit sides with protesters and Rajoelina is impeached.
Randrianirina is sworn in as head of state and promises elections within two years.
The government submits its Refondation programme and roadmap to SADC.
Randrianirina dismisses the prime minister and all ministers without explanation.
The AU Peace and Security Council urges respect for the 24-month calendar and the release of political detainees.
Mamitiana Rajaonarison, head of the financial intelligence unit, is named prime minister.
Gen Z figure Herizo Andriamanantena is arrested after a protest on 11 April; further arrests follow.
A SADC extraordinary summit calls for the release of political prisoners and the return of exiles.
The IPC publishes a projection of 3.72 million people in acute food insecurity for October 2026 to February 2027.
The IMF Board completes two reviews and releases about $155 million.
Amnesty reports at least 20 arbitrary political detentions a year after the takeover.
The High Constitutional Court backs holding the referendum before the presidential election.
In Antsirabe, Randrianirina acknowledges that the national consultation is behind schedule.
Randrianirina receives a SADC delegation led by Joyce Banda at Iavoloha.

scores.coverage_basis: AFP and Reuters file on Madagascar around turning points such as the cabinet dismissal and the anniversary of the takeover [8][12]. Antananarivo dailies publish daily on the transition, but this draft found little steady wire flow, and ISS, IDOS and ARI supply the research [2][10][24].

severity.basis: The UN counted at least 22 deaths in the first days of the 2025 protests, and this draft found no ongoing armed conflict, though ACLED data were not read [13].
The IPC projects 3.72 million people in acute food insecurity and about 502,000 children with acute malnutrition, and Midi Madagasikara warns of an extreme El Nino [5][33].
Amnesty counts at least 20 political detainees and RSF notes government-directed state broadcasters, while a cybercrime bill is pending [11][17].
AFP cites about 80 percent of people living on less than $2.15 a day, and the IMF projects inflation of 9.3 percent in 2026 with tax collection well short of targets [12][29].
Activists say the core demands on power and water are unmet and the consultation is late, while the IMF programme stays on track and growth is projected to improve [12][2][29].

parts.basis: AFP reports Rajoelina left on a French military plane, that Madagascar keeps ties with France, and that a Russian military partnership including Africa Corps training is growing; this draft read no source on US or Chinese deals [12].
No trade or commodity data were read for this draft; the IMF projects growth of 3.8 percent in 2026 and AFP says the French firm EDF is involved in the Volobe dam project [29][12].
Madagascar is an island with no land border, and ISS worries mainly about precedent for juntas elsewhere, while Midi Madagasikara warns of internal displacement from El Nino [10][33].
No diaspora or migration data were read, and the humanitarian need described by the IPC is largely inside the country [5].
The AU suspended Madagascar while SADC did not, which ISS calls a gamble, and IDOS says the case shows youth protests can topple a regime without guaranteeing democratic reform [3][10][24].

summary: Madagascar scores low on global implications because it is an island with modest trade weight in this draft and little spillover, but its case tests how the AU and SADC treat a military takeover that followed a popular uprising [10][3].
The great-power score rests on AFP's reporting of French and Russian ties, and is provisional because no source on trade, mining or US and Chinese interests was read [12].
gi.up: A stalled transition that leads the AU to sanction Madagascar or SADC to suspend it, or a Russian basing arrangement, would raise the score.
gi.down: A credible referendum and presidential election in 2027 that returns the AU and SADC to normal relations would lower it.

gaps: Crisis Group: its Madagascar page returned only older reports and no 2025 or 2026 output was read. ACLED: no Madagascar-specific 2025 or 2026 analysis was found, so the violence score rests on UN, AP and Amnesty material and is provisional.

Local sourcing leans on L'Express de Madagascar, Midi Madagasikara and Newsmada, several read through AllAfrica relays. 2424.mg, Madagascar Tribune and RFI Malagasy pages were not opened, and no TVM, RNM or ANTA page was read; RSF is the only source on state control of TVM and RNM. Several L'Express pages print no day, so their dates are given by month.

The water-cuts source comes through AllAfrica with no named outlet, byline or date, and the Jirama contract argument rests on one commentary. No Jirama financial statement or independent power producer was read.

Death toll: the UN count of at least 22 (29 September 2025) and a Gen Z spokesperson's at least 28 differ, and no later UN or official figure was read. The takeover date also varies by source (ISS says 12 October, Al Jazeera 14 October); this page uses the 17 October swearing-in.

Economic figures come from the IMF, AFP and an interview; World Bank documents were not opened. AFP's $180 million frozen IMF funds and the IMF's $155 million release were not reconciled, and electricity access is given as 36 percent (ARI) and 39 percent (IDOS citing the World Bank).

The government's response to Amnesty's findings, the status of the August cybercrime bill, and the outcome of the AU field mission were not found. The Volobe and Sahofika hydropower projects, mining, vanilla and trade were not researched, so the economic reach score is provisional.
No podcast episode, documentary or photo essay on Madagascar was verified, and only two books were checked.
